newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, facing problems at home, looks to Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, facing problems at home, looks to Belarus.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is set this week to forge closer ties with Russia's Slav ally Belarus, countering a trend of hesitation over integration among most other former Soviet republics.

Yeltsin and Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko are due to sign documents in Moscow on Wednesday which officials say will help bring their two countries closer together. Details of the documents have not been announced.

Their drive for rapid integration contrasts with the mood of other members of the loose Commonwealth of Independent States who appeared divided on many issues at a summit of the 12-nation group in Moscow last Friday.
"Yes, the question really arose at our session, how can we move forward? Nevertheless, we later reached the common conclusion that the Commonwealth was necessary," Yeltsin said after the summit.
Yeltsin, 66, appears to believe forging better ties with Belarus is a trump card because many Russians are nostalgic for the Soviet Union which fell apart in 1991.

The drive for integration with Russia's less wealthy western neighbour of about 10 million people could also deflect attention from the economic problems which prompted nationwide protests last Thursday and play into his political foes' hands.

The trade unions which organised Thursday's protests said 20 million people had taken part, but all other estimates put the total at a fraction of this. The Interior Ministry said 1.8 million people had protested across Russia.
Whatever the turnout in a country of 150 million people, the demonstrations signalled discontent with government policies that have left many people unpaid for months.
"What is important is that people took to the streets and it is time to settle accounts with them," the newspaper Rabochaya Trubuna wrote.
An opinion poll published on Sunday showed 68 percent of respondents believed recent events had shown that the country is in general heading up a dead-end street.

The poll, carried out by the independent research group VTsIOM and published in the weekly newspaper Interfax-Argumenty i Fakty, showed only 14 percent of the 1,630 respondents thought Russia was going the right way. Eighteen percent were undecided.

The poll, conducted from March 14 to 19, also showed that Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov would win most support if a presidential election were held immediately and Yeltsin did not run -- he cannot seek a third term under the constitution.

Zyuganov won 18 percent support and tough-talking Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's ousted security adviser and now a critic of his policies, was second with 15 percent backing. Liberal Grigory Yavlinsky trailed in third place with six percent support.

Some analysts also see integration with Belarus as a counterweight to NATO's plans to expand eastwards by taking in members from eastern and central Europe, the most difficult foreign policy issue facing Yeltsin.

Russia still opposes NATO expansion but Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said in Bonn at the weekend that he hoped the "negative" effects would be neutralised by an accord Moscow and the Western alliance are working on to map out their relations.
